catalog_quote: Mandan has a robustly predictable system of primary stress assignment. Primary stress is iambic and weight-sensitive, so primary stress typically appears on the second syllable, unless the first syllable is heavy, in which case the word has first-syllable stress. There is no primary stress on the third syllable or beyond. Words containing a single light syllable can still bear primary stress, so we can tell that footing for primary stress does not cross word boundaries ... Stress in Mandan is robustly drawn to the second syllable when a word begins with two light syllables, but when the first when the word begins with a heavy syllable, then that heavy syllable takes stress. ... audit.reasoning: The classification (left-aligned weight-sensitive iamb: second-syllable stress unless the first syllable is heavy = long vowel or coda glottal stop; window of two; secondary iambs to the right; preverbs as listed exception) matches Kasak 2024 §3.6.4 exactly, and every quoted fragment was verified verbatim at the cited pages in the open-access PDF we hold/text. The deciding source is a 2024 comprehensive reference grammar that itself surveys and supersedes all prior stress descriptions; Glottolog's descriptive list and a Crossref query show nothing better. no reclassification, no re-read needed; list of works to obtain limited to one low-priority older primary (Hollow 1970) for completeness only. Nothing was downloaded, so no our files was created.
